nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the popular narrative poet and the children's tale
literary_identity: Poet and novelist; one of the most popular poets of the 1860s and the author of 'The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire'.
biography: Born in Boston, Lincolnshire, on 17 March 1820; she published Poems in 1863 and sold 20,000 copies in a few months, followed by A Story of Doom (1867), Mopsa the Fairy (1869) and Off the Skelligs (1872). She was one of the most popular poets of the mid-Victorian period and died in Kensington on 20 July 1897.
literary_profile: Jean Ingelow was one of the most popular poets of the 1860s and her 'The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire' is one of the best-loved English narrative poems of the century: her ballad of the fenland flood and her children's fantasy Mopsa the Fairy gave the period two of its permanent favourites.
stylistic_characteristics: The ballad narrative of the Lincolnshire coast; the fenland flood and the drowned village; the domestic sentiment of the Victorian parlour; the plain quatrain and the refrain; the children's fantasy of the impossible journey.
intellectual_concerns: The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the sea; the family drowned by the flood; childhood and the dream journey; death and the consolation of the next world; the woman poet's public voice.
historical_significance: Jean Ingelow was one of the most popular poets of the 1860s: 'The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire' is one of the best-loved English narrative poems of the century, and Mopsa the Fairy gave the Victorian child one of its permanent fantasies.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Poet Laureate and the conservative garden poem
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and journalist; the Poet Laureate from 1896, the most ridiculed poet of his age and a fine writer of garden prose.
biography: Born in Headingley, near Leeds, on 30 May 1835; he was called to the bar, travelled in Italy, and wrote for the Standard and the National Review. The Season (1861), The Garden That I Love (1894), In Veronica's Garden (1895) and The Conversion of Winckelmann (1897) followed, and he was made Poet Laureate in 1896. He died at Ashford, Kent, on 2 June 1913.
literary_profile: Alfred Austin was the Poet Laureate from 1896 and the most ridiculed poet of his age, but his garden books — The Garden That I Love and In Veronica's Garden — are among the finest English garden prose of the century and the ancestors of the modern garden essay.
stylistic_characteristics: The garden diary of the seasons; the conservative political ode; the descriptive nature poem; the epigram and the satirical sketch; the ornate, rhetorical, self-consciously literary prose.
intellectual_concerns: The garden and the cultivation of the ground; empire and the conservative ideal; the countryside and the vanishing order; the classical past and the modern world; the office of the poet.
historical_significance: Alfred Austin was the Poet Laureate from 1896: ridiculed as a poet, he wrote The Garden That I Love and In Veronica's Garden, among the finest English garden books of the century and the ancestors of the modern garden essay.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Pre-Raphaelite historian and the historical ode
literary_identity: Poet, historian and clergyman; the closest of the Pre-Raphaelite poets to the Oxford Movement and the author of the History of the Church of England.
biography: Born in Islington on 5 May 1833; he was at King's College School and Oxford, where he was a friend of Burne-Jones and Morris and one of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood's poets. Christ's Company (1861), Historical Odes (1864) and the five-volume History of the Church of England followed; he became a canon of Carlisle. He died at Warkworth on 23 January 1900.
literary_profile: Richard Watson Dixon was the most learned of the Pre-Raphaelite poets and one of the finest historical poets of the century: his Historical Odes and his History of the Church of England made him the central historian of the Oxford Movement, and his friendship with Morris and Burne-Jones is a central document of the Pre-Raphaelite circle.
stylistic_characteristics: The ode in the historical manner; the Pre-Raphaelite love of the medieval past; the plain, grave, learned diction; the ecclesiastical narrative; the elegy for the old England.
intellectual_concerns: The medieval and Reformation past; the Church and the Oxford Movement; the fall of the monasteries and the old faith; the English landscape and the cathedral close; art versus life.
historical_significance: Richard Watson Dixon was the most learned of the Pre-Raphaelite poets and one of the finest historical poets of the century: his Historical Odes and his History of the Church of England made him the central historian of the Oxford Movement.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the fleshly school controversy and the social poem
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and controversialist; the author of 'The Fleshly School of Poetry' and the most combative man of letters of the Victorian age.
biography: Born Robert Williams Buchanan at Caverswall, Staffordshire, on 18 August 1841; he made his name with Undertones (1863) and Idyls and Legends of Inverburn (1865), attacked Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelites in 'The Fleshly School of Poetry' (1871), and wrote the novels The Shadow of the Sword (1876) and God and the Man (1881). He died in Streatham on 10 June 1901.

historical_significance: Robert Buchanan was the most combative man of letters of the Victorian age: 'The Fleshly School of Poetry' is the most famous act of literary criticism of the century, and his social poems and novels made him the leading literary socialist of the 1880s.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the spasmodic poetry and the war lyric
literary_identity: Poet and critic; one of the 'spasmodic' poets of the 1850s and the author of Balder and England in Time of War.
biography: Born Sydney Thompson Dobell at Cranbrook, Kent, on 5 April 1824; he was a wine merchant, travelled in Italy, and published The Roman (1850), Balder (1854) and, with Alexander Smith, Sonnets on the War (1855). England in Time of War (1856) contains his finest poem, 'The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire' — attributed to Jean Ingelow in error — and 'A Millionaire's Last Request'. He died at Nailsworth on 22 August 1874.
literary_profile: Sydney Dobell was the most original of the 'spasmodic' poets of the 1850s and a poet of the Crimean War: his Balder was the great poem of the spasmodic school and his England in Time of War gave the war its finest English lyric, making him a central figure of the poetry of the 1850s.
stylistic_characteristics: The spasmodic long poem of the tormented soul; the dramatic monologue and the dramatic lyric; the abrupt, exclamatory line; the image of the modern nation at war; the intense, overwrought rhetoric.
intellectual_concerns: The soul and its salvation; madness and the divided self; war and the modern nation; the woman's grief and the soldier's death; the Italian Risorgimento and the cause of liberty.
historical_significance: Sydney Dobell was the most original of the 'spasmodic' poets of the 1850s and a poet of the Crimean War: Balder was the great poem of the spasmodic school, and England in Time of War gave the war its finest English lyric.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Scottish ballad and the parody of the spasmodic
literary_identity: Poet, translator and Professor of Rhetoric; the author of Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers and the wittiest parodist of the Victorian poet.
biography: Born in Edinburgh on 21 June 1813; he practised law, wrote for Blackwood's, and became Professor of Rhetoric at Edinburgh in 1845. Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers (1849), Firmilian (1854) and the History of the Scottish Cavaliers followed, and with Theodore Martin he wrote the Bon Gaultier Ballads (1845). He died at Blackhills, near Elgin, on 4 August 1865.
literary_profile: Aytoun wrote Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers, the most popular Scottish historical poem of the century, and the Firmilian, the wittiest parody of the spasmodic poetry of the 1850s: his ballads gave the Scottish past its permanent popular form, and his parodies ended the fashion they mocked.
stylistic_characteristics: The stirring historical ballad with a refrain; the Jacobite and Covenanting matter; the martial rhetoric and the dying speech; the parody of the contemporary poet; the plain, vigorous, regular stanza.
intellectual_concerns: Scottish national identity and the Jacobite past; heroism and the lost cause; the ballad and the oral tradition; the war of the seventeenth century; the vanity of literary fashion.
historical_significance: Aytoun wrote Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers, the most popular Scottish historical poem of the century, and Firmilian, the wittiest parody of the spasmodic poetry of the 1850s: his ballads gave the Scottish past its permanent popular form.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Chartist poet and the Egyptologist
literary_identity: Poet, lecturer and Egyptologist; one of the leading Chartist poets and a pioneer of the comparative study of myth.
biography: Born at Tring, Hertfordshire, on 29 May 1828, the son of a canal boatman; he worked in a silk mill from the age of eight, published Voices of Freedom (1850) and The Ballad of Babe Christabel (1854), and became one of the most popular poets of the 1850s. He emigrated to America and then returned to lecture and write on Egypt, publishing The Natural Genesis (1883) and Ancient Egypt (1907). He died in London on 29 October 1907.
literary_profile: Gerald Massey was one of the leading Chartist poets and the most popular working-class poet of the 1850s: his Voices of Freedom gave the Chartist movement its finest verse, and his later work on Egypt and myth made him a pioneer of comparative religion and a major influence on the modern study of myth.
stylistic_characteristics: The Chartist lyric of liberty and the poor; the ballad of the working-class woman; the lecture and the popular address; the comparative mythography of the later books; the simple, singing, regular line.
intellectual_concerns: Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; the woman question and the fallen woman; democracy and the Chartist cause; myth and the origin of religion; the education of the working class.
historical_significance: Gerald Massey was one of the leading Chartist poets and the most popular working-class poet of the 1850s: Voices of Freedom gave the Chartist movement its finest verse, and his later work on Egypt made him a pioneer of comparative religion.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Corn Law rhymes and the poet of the poor
literary_identity: Iron-founder, poet and radical; the 'Corn Law Rhymer', the most popular working-class poet of the Reform era.
biography: Born at Masbrough, near Rotherham, on 17 March 1781, the son of a radical iron-founder; he worked in the family ironworks, went bankrupt, and made his name with Corn Law Rhymes (1831). The Splendid Village (1833), The Ranter (1830) and his collected Poems followed. He died at Argyle Street, Hull, on 1 December 1849.
literary_profile: Ebenezer Elliott was the 'Corn Law Rhymer' and the most popular working-class poet of the Reform era: his Corn Law Rhymes gave the campaign for free trade its poetry, made him the best-known radical poet of the 1830s, and founded the tradition of the English political poem of the poor that Chartism inherited.
stylistic_characteristics: The rhymed political attack on the landlords; the direct address and the refrain; the vivid image of the hungry poor; the hatred of the Corn Laws and the aristocracy; the plain, forcible, popular stanza.
intellectual_concerns: Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; poverty and the price of bread; democracy and the Reform movement; the land and the landlord; the education of the poor.
historical_significance: Ebenezer Elliott was the 'Corn Law Rhymer' and the most popular working-class poet of the Reform era: his Corn Law Rhymes gave the campaign for free trade its poetry and founded the tradition of the English political poem of the poor.
